title: Our Nearest Neighbour Alone
sub: The closest single star to the Sun
blurb: Six light-years away in Ophiuchus burns a small red dwarf. Only the three suns of Alpha Centauri lie closer — which makes Barnard's Star the nearest star that stands on its own, and, as of 2025, a star with four small worlds to call its own.

title: A Sixth of a Sun
blurb: Barnard's Star carries about 16% of the Sun's mass inside 19% of its width — barely above the line where a star can burn hydrogen at all. It sheds roughly a three-hundredth of the Sun's light, most of it infrared, from a surface only about 3,200 K hot.

title: Too Faint to See
blurb: For all its nearness, Barnard's Star shines at magnitude 9.5 — some sixteen times fainter than the dimmest star an unaided eye can catch. You need binoculars at the very least, which is why nobody picked it out until 1916.

title: Older Than the Sun
sub: A relic from the young galaxy
blurb: Its metal-poor chemistry and its plunging path through the galaxy mark Barnard's Star as one of the old ones — perhaps ten billion years old, more than twice the Sun's age. It was already ancient when the Earth was still a disc of dust.

title: The Old Star Still Erupts
blurb: Ancient red dwarfs are supposed to have settled down. In 1998 astronomers watched Barnard's Star throw out a flare that briefly doubled its brightness, and ultraviolet eyes have caught more since — hard news for anything trying to hold onto an atmosphere nearby.

title: The Fastest Star in Our Sky
blurb: Every star drifts, but Barnard's Star bolts. It shifts 10.4 arcseconds a year against the background — the largest proper motion of any star we know, and the reason it has been called Barnard's Runaway Star ever since 1916.

title: A Moon-Width in a Lifetime
sub: Fast for a star, slow for a person
blurb: Ten arcseconds a year sounds furious until you measure it against the full Moon, which spans about half a degree. At its pace Barnard's Star needs some 180 years to cross that little disc — a crossing it began before photography could record it.

title: It Is Coming Closer
sub: Nearest of all, around the year 11,800
blurb: Barnard's Star is falling toward us at about 110 kilometres a second. In roughly ten thousand years it will pass within 3.75 light-years and briefly become the closest star to the Sun — nearer than Proxima Centauri is today — before sweeping away again.

title: The Planets That Were Not
sub: A decade-long wobble that turned out to be the telescope
blurb: From 1963 Peter van de Kamp reported a wobble in the star's path and claimed one, then two, Jupiter-like planets. Others could not see it. By 1973 the culprit was found: the wobble tracked adjustments made to his own telescope, not any world.

title: A Real World at Last
sub: Found in 2024, after sixty years of false starts
blurb: Reading the star's light for shifts of barely thirty centimetres a second, the ESPRESSO spectrograph in Chile picked out a genuine tug: Barnard b, a world roughly a third of Earth's mass, whipping around the star every 3.15 days.

title: Four Worlds Smaller Than Earth
sub: A whole system inside a week
blurb: In 2025 a second instrument confirmed that first planet and turned up three more. Barnard b, c, d and e each weigh a fifth to a third of Earth, and every one completes its orbit in between two and seven days — the entire system fits inside a single week.

title: All Four Sit Too Close
sub: The temperate band lies far beyond them
blurb: A star this cool keeps its habitable zone tucked in tight — but Barnard's four worlds huddle tighter still, orbiting well inside even that. All of them are too warm for liquid water to last, so if a temperate world circles this star, we have not found it yet.

title: The Starship Aimed Here
blurb: Through the 1970s the British Interplanetary Society designed Daedalus, a fusion-driven probe meant to prove on paper that interstellar flight was possible. The target they picked was Barnard's Star — a fifty-year crossing at an eighth of the speed of light.

title: Six Light-Years Away
sub: Second on the list of nearest stars
blurb: Only Alpha Centauri's three suns lie between us and Barnard's Star. Its light takes just under six years to reach us — the nearest thing to a next-door star that we can study entirely on its own, and still 56 trillion kilometres out of reach.
